question: Is there a self (ātman, puruṣa, jīva) — an enduring conscious subject distinct from body and changing cognitions — or only a stream of impersonal factors designated 'person'?

sides.position: There is a self: an eternal, all-pervading substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognitions; cognition, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure and pain are its qualities and the marks by which it is known. To think 'the self does not exist' is itself a form of the false knowledge that binds.
arguments: Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition need a substrate; they are the marks (liṅga) of the self (NS 1.1.10).
One object is grasped by sight and by touch, so the grasper is other than either sense (NS 3.1.1); what the left eye saw the other recognizes (NS 3.1.7).

Memory and recognition require the same knower at two times; a series of momentary cognitions could not remember what another cognized (NS 3.1.13-14; Uddyotakara; Udayana's Ātmatattvaviveka refutes momentariness first).
A newborn's joy, fear and grief follow on memory of a former life (NS 3.1.18).
If the self were the body there would be no sin in burning a body (NS 3.1.4).

sides.position: The self is not perceived by ordinary perception but inferred: breathing in and out, the closing and opening of the eyes, life, the movement of the mind, the functioning of the other senses, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort are its marks; the word 'I' applies to it, not to the body; selves are many, since their states differ.

A self distinct from body and cognition exists — the agent who enjoys the fruit of sacrifice in another world; without it the injunctions for heaven would be pointless. Kumārila: the self is known in the notion 'I'; Prabhākara: it shines forth in every cognition as its knower, never as its object.

Puruṣa exists: aggregates exist for the sake of another; there must be something opposite to what has the three guṇas; there must be a controller, an enjoyer, and one for whose isolation activity takes place. Puruṣas are many, since birth, death and the instruments are allotted to each separately.

The seer is seeing alone, which appears to conform to the mind's cognitions; the mind is not self-illuminating, because it is seen; if one cognition were grasped by another there would be infinite regress and confusion of memories; a mind that were only momentary cognitions could not be made one-pointed.

The self is the self-evident witness (sākṣin) of all cognitions, never an object and never deniable — no one thinks 'I am not'. Body, senses, breath, mind and intellect, and the agent-enjoyer, are not-self, superimposed on it. Against the Buddhists: memory and recognition ('I saw that, I see this') show one enduring knower; a momentary store-consciousness cannot hold impressions; the witness is not a momentary cognition.

texts.ref: refutation of mistaken views of the self

sides.position: The self is a distinct, eternal, atomic knower, established in the awareness 'I', self-luminous; consciousness is its attribute, which belongs to someone and is of something — not the self itself; each self is a mode of Brahman.

The soul (jīva) exists; its defining mark is cognitive activity (upayoga); it is the doer and enjoyer of its karma, can be liberated, and is eternal as substance but non-eternal as mode (its states and births). One-sided permanence (as of the Naiyāyikas) and one-sided momentariness (as of the Buddhists) are both refuted.

There is a soul within the body and distinct from it: it says 'not this' of each thing, speaks of 'my body', knows through the senses, and knows on waking that it slept; souls are many, their experience, bondage and release differing.

Against the Buddhist that only momentary cognitions appear and no permanent seer: memory is impossible if the remembering cognition is separate from the experience; the unity of cognitions at different times is the one conscious subject, Maheśvara, endowed with the powers of knowing, remembering and excluding.

Each of the five aggregates is not-self: were it self it would not lead to affliction and one could say 'let it be thus'; what is impermanent and painful is not fit to be regarded 'this is mine, this I am, this is my self'. 'Being' is a designation, as 'chariot' is for assembled parts. Asked 'is there a self? is there no self?' the Buddha was silent: either answer would side with eternalism or annihilationism.

The person is not found as a real and ultimate fact; 'Nāgasena' and 'chariot' are designations; as the chariot is not found when each part is examined, there is no being in the ultimate sense, only mentality-materiality.

texts.ref: the chariot dialogue (locator as in tea:milindapanha:3.1.1)

sides.position: Apart from the series of aggregates there is no self; 'self' designates the series. Those outside this teaching are not liberated because they hold 'self' to be a separate entity rather than a designation for the series (Vasubandhu, AKBh ch. 9); only aggregates, conditioned by defilement and karma, enter the womb through the intermediate existence, like a flame.

One who sees a self loves it as 'I', thirsts for its happiness, and that thirst hides faults and drives rebirth: the view of self is the root of saṃsāra. The selves of the Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, Sāṃkhyas, Jains, Upaniṣadic thinkers and Vātsīputrīyas are examined and refuted; whatever exists is momentary.

If the self were the aggregates it would arise and perish; if other than them it would lack their marks. The self is neither the aggregates, nor other than them, nor their possessor — like the chariot sought in seven ways. The Buddhas have taught 'self', have taught 'no-self', and have taught neither self nor no-self; 'I exist' and 'mine exists' are false in the ultimate sense.

A person (pudgala) exists, designated in dependence on the present aggregates, neither the same as nor different from them, inexpressible — as fire in dependence on fuel; it is the bearer of the burden of the aggregates (the middle position; see dsp:pudgala).

'Self' in the true sense means the tathāgatagarbha: all beings have buddha-nature; seeing the Tathāgata as impermanent, suffering, non-self and impure is inverted; the dharmakāya has the perfection of self. (Other Mahāyāna texts read this 'self' as a skilful name for emptiness — see dsp:buddha-nature-self-or-emptiness.)
(As reported) Only the living body qualified by consciousness; nothing survives it.
(As reported) Pakudha: the soul is one of seven eternal, unmoving bodies.
(As reported) Not declared: 'who knows whether the soul exists?'
A self distinct from the body exists: consciousness is absent in the corpse.

historical_debates.name: The Nyāya–Buddhist exchange on the self (textual)
historical_debates.accounts: Nyāyabhāṣya and Nyāyavārttika on NS 3.1; Pramāṇavārttika; Tattvasaṅgraha (Ātmaparīkṣā); Ātmatattvaviveka; Ratnakīrti's Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds that its own arguments stand; the exchange continued until Buddhism waned in India.
historical_debates.notes: A series of written replies across generations, not a single meeting.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: all parties agree that the body, senses and changing cognitions are not the true self, but they disagree whether anything beyond them — an enduring conscious subject — exists.
reconciliation.detail: Partial convergences recorded without reconciling: (a) Advaita, Sāṃkhya-Yoga and the Buddhists all deny that the agent-ego or the aggregates are the self; (b) the Jains offer their own standpoint synthesis — the soul permanent as substance, changing as mode (Bhagavatī 7.2; Āptamīmāṃsā 3); (c) Kṣemarāja places every doctrine of the self as a role of the one consciousness at a particular level (Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya 8). None of these is accepted by the other parties.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Buddhist logicians refute every permanent self, the Upaniṣadic one included (Tattvasaṅgraha, Ātmaparīkṣā); Theravāda and Vasubandhu reject even a person neither same nor different from the aggregates; Nyāya counts denial of the self as false knowledge (NBh 1.1.2); Advaita denies that its witness is the Buddhist's momentary cognition (BSBh 2.2.28); Madhyamaka rejects both 'self' and 'no-self' as fixed views (MMK 18.6).

candidate_readings: P1-level: the Buddhist analysis negates a self found among or apart from the aggregates — which Advaita also calls not-self — while Advaita's witness is said never to be an object of such analysis. Rejected by Śāntarakṣita (who refutes the Upaniṣadic self too) and by Advaita (which asserts the self as being-consciousness, not an absence).

P2-standpoint (the Jains' own synthesis): permanent from the substance standpoint, momentary from the mode standpoint, so the Nyāya and Buddhist theses each state one aspect. Rejected by both Nyāya and the Buddhists as combining incompatible claims.

P4-stage (Kṣemarāja, PH 8): each doctrine of the self is a role of the one consciousness reached at a given level — body, buddhi, prāṇa, void, prakṛti, Īśvara. An inclusivist ranking that the ranked schools do not accept.
P5-neyartha: Mahāyāna passages on a 'true self' (tathāgatagarbha) read as provisional by some, definitive by others (see dsp:buddha-nature-self-or-emptiness).

P6-upaya: the Buddha's silence to Vacchagotta (SN 44.10) and MMK 18.6 ('self' and 'no-self' both taught) read as teaching fitted to the hearer; Nyāya and Advaita do not accept that their self is merely a teaching device.
notes: Owned by U50. Cārvāka, Ajñāna and Pakudha sides (as reported by opponents) were contributed by U33 and are included verbatim. The Pudgalavāda middle position is treated fully in dsp:pudgala (U38).

question: Does the effect pre-exist in its cause (satkārya), is it newly produced (asatkārya/ārambha), is it an apparent transformation of an unchanging cause (vivarta), a real manifestation of consciousness (ābhāsa), a transformation of God that leaves him unchanged (avikṛta-pariṇāma), or dependently arisen and ultimately unarisen?

sides.position: The effect exists in its material cause before it is produced (satkārya): because what does not exist cannot be produced; because a definite material cause is taken for a definite effect; because not everything arises from everything; because a capable cause produces only what it is capable of; because the effect has the nature of its cause. Production is manifestation.

Past and future exist in their own form, differing in their time-paths; change is transformation of property, time-mark and state in an enduring substrate; the instrumental cause does not set the material causes going but only removes the obstruction, as a farmer breaches a dyke.

The effect is a new thing, non-existent before production (asatkārya, ārambhavāda): before it is produced the fruit is not existent in the Sāṃkhya sense, for existence and non-existence are opposed; it comes about from inherent, non-inherent and instrumental causes and is the counterpositive of its prior absence. Nor does existence arise from non-existence as such (the sprout from the destroyed seed).
From the absence of the cause follows the absence of the effect, not the reverse; a thing before it is produced is non-existent (prior absence) — the effect is a newly made whole.

The effect is non-different from its cause, 'a verbal handle, a name' — as pots are only clay (CU 6.1.4; BS 2.1.14). Brahman is both material and efficient cause; the world is its apparent transformation (vivarta), not a real modification (vikāra): the snake is only the rope. From the highest standpoint nothing whatever is born.

Brahman is both the material and the efficient cause; the world is non-different from Brahman as pots from clay, but the effect is a real state of Brahman, whose body is the sentient and non-sentient; real transformation (pariṇāma) touches Brahman's body, not its essence.
Brahman makes itself into the world by real transformation of its power (ātmakṛteḥ pariṇāmāt); the effect is real, both different and non-different from its cause (Bhāskara; Nimbārka).
Brahman, transforming itself, is the material cause of the world, yet this transformation involves no change in Brahman (avikṛta-pariṇāma).

Viṣṇu is the independent cause who creates, maintains, dissolves and controls; the world is real and its material is prakṛti, dependent on him; the doctrine of apparent transformation is refuted, since the witness establishes what is real.

Things that appear in the present as external are possible only if they already exist within consciousness; the Lord, by his will and infinite powers, makes them appear (ābhāsa) — this is his creatorhood. Consciousness, free, is the cause of the universe, which she unfolds on her own screen: a real self-manifestation, not an illusion.

The world, spoken of as 'he, she and it', undergoes origination, maintenance and dissolution, so it has an agent; it resolves into and re-emerges from its cause — Śiva as efficient cause working through real māyā as material.
Formations occur through ignorance and the other conditions; the wheel of becoming has no maker such as a Brahmā: things arise dependently, neither from a self-made nor an other-made cause.

No existent whatever is ever found arisen from itself, from another, from both, or without a cause (MMK 1.1); the effect is neither made of the conditions nor of non-conditions; dependent arising is itself emptiness, and emptiness, dependent origination and the middle way have one meaning.

The existent is endowed at once with origination, cessation and persistence: a thing is in some respect existent and in some respect non-existent before its production. Time, own-nature, destiny, former deeds and human effort, each held one-sidedly as the cause, are wrong views; taken together they are right view.

Brahman, without beginning or end, whose essence is the Word, appears (vivartate) as objects; the world is the Word-principle's appearing (Bhartṛhari — the earliest use of vivarta as a technical term recorded here).
Time, own-nature, fixed order, chance, the elements, the womb and the person are weighed as causes and none suffices; it is the greatness of God in the world by which the wheel of Brahman turns.

historical_debates.name: The commentarial exchange on MMK 1.1
historical_debates.accounts: Buddhapālita-vṛtti 1.1; Prajñāpradīpa 1.1; Prasannapadā 1.1 (see dsp:prasangika-svatantrika)

historical_debates.name: Sāṃkhya and its critics on the pre-existent effect (textual)
historical_debates.date: c. early centuries CE onward (scholarly, approximate)
historical_debates.accounts: Sāṃkhyakārikā 9; Nyāyasūtra 4.1.48-50; Madhyamakahṛdaya 6; Brahmasūtra 2.1.14-20 and 2.2.1-10
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds its own account of causation; Vedānta adopts the non-difference of effect from cause while rejecting Sāṃkhya's unconscious pradhāna.

reconciliation.explanation: Partly reconciled by the traditions' own devices: Advaita and Madhyamaka accept causal change or dependent arising at the conventional level while denying real origination ultimately (P1), and the Jains hold the pre-existence and the novelty of the effect true from the substance and mode standpoints (P2); the Sāṃkhya–Nyāya and vivarta–ābhāsa disagreements are not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: P1: Śaṅkara uses the language of transformation for the empirical world and non-difference/vivarta for the ultimate (BSBh 2.1.14; Vedāntasāra's vikāra–vivarta verse); Nāgārjuna negates the four modes of arising while affirming dependent arising as emptiness (MMK 1.1; VV 71). P2: the Jain triad of origination, cessation and persistence (TS 5.30) and Siddhasena's rule that each single cause held one-sidedly is wrong view (Sanmati 3.53) are the Jains' own reconciliation. What remains: whether the effect's pre-existence is literal (Sāṃkhya) or incoherent (Nyāya); whether the world's appearance is real manifestation of consciousness (Kashmir Śaivism) or indeterminable superimposition (Advaita); whether Brahman's transformation is real (Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhedābheda, Vallabha) or apparent.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya rejects satkārya outright (NS 4.1.48-50) and Sāṃkhya asatkārya (SK 9); Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhedābheda, Vallabha and Dvaita deny that the world's transformation is merely apparent (Śrībhāṣya 2.1.15; Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.95-98); Kashmir Śaivism holds manifestation real, not vivarta; Madhyamaka rejects the Jain 'both' as a mode of arising already negated (MMK 1.1).

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint for Sāṃkhya vs Nyāya: satkārya speaks of the material cause's capacity (the substance standpoint), asatkārya of the product as a new whole (the mode standpoint) — rejected by both, each of whom argues the other's thesis is incoherent.

P1-level for Advaita vs Kashmir Śaivism: both deny change in the ultimate consciousness; they differ on whether the appearance is real self-display (ābhāsa) or indeterminable (vivarta) — the Trika insists on the reality of manifestation, Advaita on its sublatability.
P1-level for Advaita vs the theistic Vedāntas: transformation (pariṇāma) true empirically, vivarta true ultimately — rejected by Rāmānuja, Nimbārka, Vallabha and Madhva, who deny degrees of reality.
notes: Scholarly observation (metadata only): the term vivarta is used by Bhartṛhari before its Advaita use.

question: Is the world real, or an appearance (mithyā) that is neither real nor unreal, superimposed on the one reality — and is māyā an indeterminable ignorance or the Lord's real power?

sides.position: The world is mithyā: not real, since it is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman; not unreal, since it appears; indeterminable as either — like the silver seen in shell. Duality is mere māyā; non-duality is the ultimate truth. Three orders are distinguished: the ultimate (Brahman), the empirical (the world, real for all practical purposes — Śaṅkara defends external objects against the Buddhist idealist), and the illusory (dream, rope-snake). Falsity is defended under five definitions against the Dvaita critique.

The world of souls and matter is real, the body of Brahman. The Advaitin's avidyā is untenable in seven ways — no locus, no power to conceal self-luminous Brahman, no coherent nature, no sense to 'indescribable', no means of knowledge, no remover, no removal; no means of knowledge establishes an undifferentiated reality; consciousness is always someone's and of something.

The world is real: the witness (sākṣin) establishes it as unsublated; what is sublated produces no effect; even dream-objects are real products of impressions. None of the five Advaita definitions of falsity is coherent, and the inferences from 'perceivable', 'insentient' and 'limited' fail. Reality is twofold: the independent (Viṣṇu) and the dependent (souls and matter) — dependent, but real.
The effect is real and both different and non-different from its cause; those who expound māyā lead people astray (Bhāskara).

The world is a real transformation of the Lord's external power; the souls are his marginal power, distinct yet dependent. To call the world false and the Lord's lordship imagined is the māyāvāda that the Gītā (16.8) describes and the Padma Purāṇa calls 'Buddhism in disguise'.

The universe is the real self-manifestation of free consciousness on its own screen; māyā is the Lord's power of self-concealment (Māyā-śakti), his supreme freedom — not an indeterminable ignorance. Those who say 'in the beginning this was being' stand at the level of the Īśvara-tattva, and some knowers of the Upaniṣads take prāṇa as the self: partial roles of the one consciousness. (The Vijñāna Bhairava nevertheless teaches contemplating the universe as a magic show as one means to peace.)
Māyā is the Goddess's own power; she is the manifest and the unmanifest; her reality is beyond both duality and non-duality (see dsp:maya-sakti-or-avidya).

The world is real, produced from real māyā by Śiva as efficient cause; 'advaita' in the Śivajñānabodha means non-separateness, not numerical identity; the Advaita and other views are set out and refuted.
The world is real, being produced by faultless causes and never sublated; bondage cannot be due to an unreal avidyā — and a real avidyā would abandon non-dualism.
Absolute non-duality is refuted: if all were one there would be no distinction of act and fruit, merit and demerit, this world and the next, knowledge and ignorance, bondage and release.
The idealist and illusionist thesis lacks a reason: the notion of dream-objects depends on prior waking experience, as memory does; false cognition presupposes a real object mistaken.

All dharmas, the fruits of the path and buddhahood itself are like an illusion, like a dream — appearing conventionally, empty of own-nature; form is emptiness and emptiness form (the Prajñāpāramitā background shared by the Mahāyāna schools).

historical_debates.name: The Nyāyāmṛta–Advaitasiddhi exchange
historical_debates.accounts: Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta attacks the Advaita definitions of falsity and the inferences for it; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it section by section; Vyāsa Rāmācārya's Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī defends the Nyāyāmṛta; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā (Gauḍabrahmānandī) defends the Advaitasiddhi; later rejoinders continued (e.g. the Nyāyāmṛta-kaṇṭakoddhāra and the Nyāyāmṛta-āmoda in the Dvaita line).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds that its own side prevailed; neither presents the exchange as closed.
historical_debates.notes: The order of the later rejoinders is given from memory (moderate confidence).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: Advaita's own levels of reality make the world real empirically and false ultimately, but Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Śaiva Siddhānta and Kashmir Śaivism reject the very distinction as applied to the world, each for its own reasons.
reconciliation.detail: Advaita offers P1 in its own terms (the world is vyāvahārika-sat; BSBh 2.2.28 upholds external objects against the Buddhist idealist). The theistic Vedāntas deny that anything can be empirically real and ultimately false (Śrībhāṣya 1.1.1; Nyāyāmṛta 1). Kashmir Śaivism agrees that the world depends on one consciousness but calls it that consciousness's real self-display and māyā its power, not avidyā — a difference both sides keep.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Rāmānuja's seven untenabilities of avidyā (Śrībhāṣya 1.1.1); Vyāsatīrtha's refutation of the five definitions of falsity (Nyāyāmṛta); Madhva's rejection of vivarta (Anuvyākhyāna 1.4.95-98); the Kashmir Śaiva view of māyā as Śakti (Paramārthasāra 15); Advaita in turn holds that any real second to Brahman contradicts the non-dual texts (MK 1.17; Advaitasiddhi).

candidate_readings: P1-level (Advaita's own): the world is real at the empirical level and false only from the standpoint of Brahman — rejected by Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita, for whom whatever is, is real, and the empirical/ultimate distinction is not scriptural.

P2-standpoint: from the side of the one consciousness there is no second, from the side of the embodied soul the world is real — rejected by Madhva and Rāmānuja, who hold the world real from every standpoint, and by Advaita if it implies that the world's reality is ultimate.

P4-stage: Kṣemarāja ranks the Vedāntins' 'being' at the Īśvara-tattva, and the Vijñāna Bhairava prescribes seeing the world as a magic show as a practice (VBT 102, 133) — a practice-level use of the 'appearance' view that does not settle its truth.
vivarta vs ābhāsa (Advaita vs Kashmir Śaivism): both deny that the one consciousness changes; they differ whether its appearing is real self-display or indeterminable — kept apart by both.

question: Are the individual souls one with Brahman/God, eternally distinct from him and from one another, or both different and non-different?

sides.position: The individual self is Brahman alone: 'that you are', 'I am Brahman', 'this self is Brahman'. The one Lord is the knower of the field in all fields; the plurality and transmigration of souls belong to adjuncts. Of the three early teachers in the Brahmasūtra, Kāśakṛtsna's view — that the supreme Lord himself abides as the individual self — is the one in accord with scripture.

Difference is real and eternal — fivefold (pañca-bheda): between the Lord and souls, the Lord and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, and matter and matter. 'Tat tvam asi' does not teach identity (it is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi', 'you are not that', or of the soul's dependence on and likeness to the Lord); those who, proud with 'I am Brahman', read the Veda as oneness go to darkness. Liberated souls remain distinct and graded.

Souls are eternal and many and are modes and body of Brahman, inseparable from him (apṛthak-siddhi). In 'tat tvam asi' both words denote Brahman — 'that' as the cause of the world, 'you' as having the soul as its body; scripture's texts of difference, of non-difference and the mediating texts are all true. The self is a part of Brahman as an attribute is part of what it qualifies; the Gītā's 'never was there a time when I was not, nor you' teaches the eternal plurality of selves.
The soul is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman, different from it by its limiting adjuncts and non-different in essence (Bhāskara: difference adventitious).

Because scripture declares both, the soul is a part of Brahman both different and non-different by nature (svābhāvika), like the snake and its coils; the released soul abides in non-separation from Brahman while remaining a distinct knower.
The souls are the Lord's marginal power, eternally distinct from yet dependent on him — inconceivable difference and non-difference (acintya-bhedābheda).

The Brahmasūtra itself records three earlier views on the passages that identify the self with Brahman: Āśmarathya (identity as the fulfilment of the promise that by knowing one all is known), Auḍulomi (identity when the soul departs in liberation), Kāśakṛtsna (the supreme self abides as the individual self). The soul is called a part 'because of the declarations of difference and otherwise'.

The Lord is one with souls and yet other than them, and with them — like the soul with the body, the vowel with the consonants; non-duality means inseparability, not identity; the liberated soul becomes equal to Śiva but remains a soul.
Maheśvara alone is the self of all beings, of the form of the universe, full of the undivided awareness 'I'; the liberated becomes (like) Śiva.
Selves are many, not one: though pleasure, pain and cognition arise alike, their distinct states (bondage, release, experience) show plurality.
Though the seen has ceased for the one whose purpose is fulfilled, it has not ceased for others, being common to them: puruṣas are many.
Asked whether there are many puruṣas or one, the Mokṣadharma reports that the Sāṃkhya-Yoga thinkers hold many, and teaches that all are grounded in the one Puruṣa.
Souls are infinitely many, each an independent substance; absolute non-duality is refuted.

historical_debates.name: Nyāyāmṛta and Advaitasiddhi on the Upaniṣadic identity sentences
historical_debates.accounts: Nyāyāmṛta ch. 2 denies that 'tat tvam asi' and 'satyaṃ jñānam anantam' convey an impartite (akhaṇḍa) meaning; the Advaitasiddhi replies (see also dsp:world-real-or-appearance).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds its own reading established.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: identity (Advaita), eternal difference (Dvaita) and qualified or natural difference-in-non-difference (Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhedābheda, Śaiva Siddhānta) are each defended as the purport of the same texts.
reconciliation.detail: The Brahmasūtra already records the plurality of readings (1.4.20-22). Advaita holds difference to be empirical; the bhedābheda schools hold difference and non-difference both real; Dvaita holds difference real in every state including release.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Madhva brands the identity reading an asura view (Chāndogya-bhāṣya 6.8.7) and holds the five differences real (MBhTN 1.68-71); Advaita holds difference due to adjuncts only (BSBh 1.4.22); Rāmānuja rejects both identity of essence and absolute difference (Vedārthasaṃgraha).

candidate_readings: P1-level (Advaita's own): difference is real for the empirical self, identity is the ultimate truth — rejected by Madhva, for whom difference is real in every state, and by Rāmānuja, who denies identity of essence.

P2-standpoint: souls one with the Lord as consciousness (substance standpoint), many as individual centres (mode standpoint) — the bhedābheda schools' own form; rejected by Dvaita as a denial of real difference and by Advaita as a denial of non-duality.

P3-path (devotional vs knowledge): the devotee's 'I am yours' (dāsoham) and the knower's 'I am that' (so'ham) as two paths — Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra 29-31 records Kāśyapa (difference), Bādarāyaṇa (identity) and Śāṇḍilya (both); rejected by Dvaita as making difference merely devotional.
P4-stage: dāsoham ripening into so'ham (see dsp:dasoham-soham) — rejected by Dvaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita, for whom the servant relation is eternal.

question: Is Advaita Vedānta — the doctrine of māyā — 'Buddhism in disguise' (pracchanna-bauddha)?

sides.position: Bhāskara: the doctrine of māyā — disputed, cut off from its root and 'sung by the Mahāyāna Buddhists' — leads people astray.

Madhva and Jayatīrtha: the māyā-teacher and the Mādhyamika are both to be ignored — what is the void for the voidist is Brahman for the māyā-teacher; both ultimates are attributeless and defined only by exclusion; the voidists' saṃvṛti is the māyā-teachers' māyā, alike beginningless, indeterminable, concealing and projecting. Liberation cannot come from knowing the void.
The Padma Purāṇa (Uttarakhaṇḍa), in Śiva's list of heretical teachings: 'māyāvāda is a false teaching, called Buddhism in disguise; I taught it in the Kali age in the form of a brāhmaṇa'.

Jīva Gosvāmī: the doctrine that the world is false and the Lord's lordship imagined by ignorance is the view the Gītā (16.8) calls godless; it conflicts with the Lord's word and is rightly called māyāvāda, which the Padma Purāṇa calls Buddhism in disguise. Caitanya (as the Gauḍīya texts present him) rejects Śaṅkara's commentary as hiding the sūtras' direct sense.
Vedānta Deśika opens the Śatadūṣaṇī urging followers of Rāmānuja's path to 'strive on every side for victory over the crypto-Buddhists (pracchanna-bauddha)'.
sides.notes: Whether Yāmuna or Rāmānuja themselves use the label 'pracchanna-bauddha' is not verified here (see REPORT).

sides.position: Vijñānabhikṣu: the māyā doctrine of the 'modern' Vedāntins is not the Brahmasūtra's teaching; with the Padma Purāṇa he counts it among heterodox (crypto-Buddhist) teachings.

Advaita is not Buddhism: Śaṅkara refutes all three Buddhist doctrines — the realist, the idealist and the void — and dismisses the void as contradicted by every means of knowledge; against the idealist he upholds external objects and the undeniable, self-established witness; memory proves one enduring knower. The non-dual reality free of knower, known and knowing 'was not spoken by the Buddha': the Buddhist denial of external objects is only near to non-duality, which is to be known from the Upaniṣads alone. Brahman is being (sat) and consciousness, the self that no one can deny — not a void and not a momentary cognition.

historical_debates.name: Caitanya and Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya at Purī
historical_debates.accounts: Caitanya-caritāmṛta Madhya 6 (the Gauḍīya tradition's account)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Gauḍīya: Sārvabhauma, after expounding Śaṅkara's reading for seven days, accepted Caitanya's and became his devotee.

doctrinal_vs_historical.note: Kept separate as the brief requires. The doctrinal charge (sides above) is that Advaita's teaching is Buddhist in substance. The historical question — borrowings of argument, simile and vocabulary between Madhyamaka/Yogācāra and Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkya-kārikā — belongs to the borrowings layer and is recorded there (U49), not decided here.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the critics hold that Advaita's attributeless Brahman and māyā equal the Buddhists' void and saṃvṛti; Advaita holds that Brahman as being-consciousness and the undeniable witness are exactly what the Buddhists deny.
reconciliation.detail: Both parties agree on some facts — Advaita and Madhyamaka each use two levels of truth, and Gauḍapāda uses Buddhist-like language — but disagree whether the difference in what is called ultimate (sat-cit vs śūnyatā) is decisive (Advaita: MK-bhāṣya 4.99; BSBh 2.2.31) or merely verbal (Jayatīrtha, Nyāyasudhā 4.2.46). The Buddhists' own view of the Upaniṣadic self is recorded in dsp:is-there-a-self (Madhyamakahṛdaya 8; Tattvasaṅgraha).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Advaita rejects the charge (BSBh 2.2.18-32; MK-bhāṣya 4.99: 'this was not spoken by the Buddha'). The critics reject the reply: Jayatīrtha says the marks of māyā and saṃvṛti are the same; Jīva Gosvāmī reads Gītā 16.8 as describing māyāvāda. Buddhist authors (Bhāviveka, Śāntarakṣita) themselves refute the Vedāntic self and would not accept Advaita as Buddhist either.

candidate_readings: P8-six-marks: read by opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise and reasoning, the purport of Śaṅkara's commentaries is the Upaniṣadic Brahman as existent (sat), which the Buddhist texts deny — Advaita's own claim; the critics apply the same marks to find māyā/void as the purport.

P1-level: both systems use a two-truths frame; the charge concerns what is placed at the ultimate — the critics treat 'attributeless' as equivalent to 'void', Advaita and the Buddhists both reject that equivalence.
P6-upaya (the Padma Purāṇa's own framing): māyāvāda as a teaching given at the Lord's command to delude the asuras — a Purāṇic account the Advaitins do not accept as describing their teaching.
notes: Correction to the unit brief: Bhāskara, Madhva/Jayatīrtha, the Padma Purāṇa (as quoted by Jīva), Jīva Gosvāmī and Vedānta Deśika are recorded with texts; the attribution of the explicit 'crypto-Buddhist' label to Yāmuna or Rāmānuja could not be verified and is not asserted; Vijñānabhikṣu is recorded at low confidence.

question: Is awakening sudden — an all-at-once seeing of the mind's nature — or gradual, reached by stages of cultivation and analysis; and after sudden awakening, is gradual cultivation still needed?

sides.position: Shenhui (Southern school): Bodhidharma's robe and the direct transmission passed to Huineng; Shenxiu's line is collateral, and its teaching — 'freezing the mind to enter samādhi, fixing the mind to view purity, activating the mind to illumine outside, concentrating the mind to realise within' — is gradual; the true teaching is sudden awakening.

The Platform Sūtra: the Dharma has no sudden or gradual; people's natures are sharp or dull — the deluded cultivate gradually, the awakened accord suddenly. Its gate takes no-thought as its tenet, no-form as its substance, non-abiding as its root; for one awakened to self-nature there is 'sudden awakening, sudden cultivation, without gradual steps', while Shenxiu's three trainings suit smaller faculties.

The Northern school in its own words: the buddhas have a great expedient for entering the Way — with one thought of the pure mind one suddenly transcends to the buddha-ground; viewing the mind, if it is pure, is called the ground of the pure mind; awakening is the mind's substance free of thought, equal to space. (The Southern texts report Shenxiu's verse — the body the bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror to be wiped — and his 'fix the mind, view stillness'.)

Moheyan (Chinese party at the Tibetan court): all beings are bound by deluded, discriminating thought; when thoughts arise, do not follow them — 'not thinking, not examining' — and the originally pure mind appears; the six perfections are included in this non-examining; entry into non-conceptuality is simultaneous, not by steps.

Kamalaśīla: there is no way other than correct analysis (bhūta-pratyavekṣā) to reach non-recollection and non-attention; mere absence of thought cannot cause non-conceptual wisdom, or one who has fainted would have it. Seeing by analysis that no dharma has arisen in the three times, the yogin enters non-conceptual wisdom; the path is gradual — calm abiding and insight, the perfections and the grounds.
The Kathāvatthu rejects the thesis that the truths are penetrated gradually (anupubbābhisamaya): each path penetrates the four truths at once.
The truths are realized in sixteen successive moments of acceptance and knowledge on the path of seeing — a graded, momentary sequence.

The Laṅkāvatāra: the stream of what is seen as one's own mind is purified gradually — as mangoes ripen — and also all at once — as a mirror shows all forms at once. The Avataṃsaka: at the first arousal of the mind one attains unsurpassed awakening. The Śūraṅgama: in principle awakening is sudden, in phenomena removal is gradual.

Zongmi: sudden and gradual, awakening and cultivation, seem opposed but accord and support one another; if one cultivates on the basis of awakening it is understanding-awakening, if one awakens through cultivation it is realization-awakening; 'first sudden awakening, then gradual cultivation' is like the sun rising at once while frost melts gradually. Over past lives there is only the gradual.

Jinul: though there are many gates, in essence they are two — sudden awakening and gradual cultivation; even the 'sudden awakening, sudden cultivation' of the highest faculties rests on gradual cultivation in past lives; the principle is awakened suddenly, habit energies are removed step by step.

(Recent) Seongcheol: the patriarchs' awakening is realization-awakening in which cultivation is also complete — sudden awakening, sudden cultivation; Jinul's formula describes only understanding-awakening.

Sakya Paṇḍita: the Mahāmudrā of his day and the 'Chinese Great Perfection' are essentially the same as the Hashang's teaching rejected in Tibet; true Mahāmudrā is the wisdom born of empowerment and the two stages.

The Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa: by the difference of persons' minds there are the gradual and the simultaneous; the medicine of one is the poison of the other — teach the simultaneous to one with the residue of former training, the gradual to beginners.

(An analogue in the Upaniṣadic yoga texts) The Varāha Upaniṣad distinguishes Śuka's path of the bird — immediate liberation through inquiry into the great sayings — from Vāmadeva's path of the ant — gradual liberation over births through yoga — and says both reach Brahman.

historical_debates.name: The Samye debate (bSam yas)
historical_debates.date: tradition: c. 792–794 CE under Khri srong lde btsan
historical_debates.accounts: Tibetan accounts (the Testament of Ba / sBa bzhed; later Bu ston and others) report a debate before the king in which the Indian party of Kamalaśīla, teaching the gradual path of the perfections, prevailed over the party of the Chinese master Moheyan, teaching sudden non-conceptuality, and the king ruled that Tibetans should follow Nāgārjuna's view and the gradual path. The Chinese Dunhuang document Dunwu dasheng zhengli jue (compiled by Wangxi) records Moheyan's answers to the Indian objections and presents his teaching as upheld. Kamalaśīla's third Bhāvanākrama argues against non-thinking as the way to non-conceptuality.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Tibetan tradition: Kamalaśīla prevailed and Moheyan left Tibet. Dunhuang Chinese account: Moheyan's teaching was vindicated. Nupchen's Samten Migdrön ranks the simultaneous above the gradual but below Mahāyoga and Atiyoga.
historical_debates.scholarly: Whether a single formal debate took place, or a series of written and oral exchanges, is disputed (scholarly account, labelled).

historical_debates.name: Shenhui's Huatai assembly
historical_debates.date: 732 CE (Kaiyuan 20), Dayun monastery at Huatai (tradition's account)
historical_debates.accounts: Putidamo nanzong ding shifei lun (record of Shenhui's challenge to the Northern school's claim to be the true line and to its 'gradual' teaching; the opponent named there is the Dharma master Chongyuan)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Heze tradition: Huineng established as the Sixth Patriarch and the Southern teaching as sudden and orthodox; the Northern school's own texts (e.g. Dasheng wusheng fangbian men) present their teaching otherwise.

historical_debates.name: Kathāvatthu 2.9 (Anupubbābhisamayakathā)
historical_debates.date: tradition: the Third Council under Aśoka
historical_debates.accounts: Kathāvatthu 2.9 and commentary
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Theravāda: gradual penetration of the truths rejected; each path penetrates all four truths at once.

historical_debates.name: Seongcheol's critique of Jinul (recent)
historical_debates.accounts: Seonmun jeongno
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Contested within Korean Seon to the present.

reconciliation.explanation: Reconciled within Chan, Seon and the tantric Tengyur by their own principle that sudden and gradual lie in the practitioner's faculties, not in the Dharma (P4-stage), and by the reading 'principle is awakened suddenly, phenomena are removed gradually' (P1-level); the Samye question — whether non-conceptuality is reached by non-examining or only through analysis — remains not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: Platform Sūtra 7.3 ('the Dharma has no sudden or gradual; people are sharp or dull'), Zongmi's ninth harmonisation and his sun-and-frost simile, Jinul's sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, the Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa's medicine-and-poison verse, and the Varāha Upaniṣad's bird and ant paths all assign the two to different kinds of practitioner or to different aspects (li and shi) of one path. The Śūraṅgama's 理則頓悟…事非頓除 is the P1 form.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kamalaśīla and the Tibetan tradition after Samye reject non-examining as a path (Bhāvanākrama 3; Sakya Paṇḍita, Domsum Rabye 3); Shenhui rejects the Northern teaching as gradual and collateral; Seongcheol (recent) rejects gradual cultivation after awakening as mere understanding-awakening; the Kathāvatthu rejects gradual penetration of the truths that the Sarvāstivāda teaches.

candidate_readings: P4-stage for Samye: the simultaneous approach for those of sharp faculties or with former training, the gradual for beginners (Ājñāsamyakpramāṇa; Samten Migdrön's ranking) — rejected by Kamalaśīla ('no way other than correct analysis').
P6-upaya: 'not thinking, not examining' as a pointer to the ever-present mind rather than a technique — not accepted by the Tibetan critics, who read it as a method that leads to dullness.
Kathāvatthu vs Sarvāstivāda: 'at once' of the path-moment vs sixteen moments of the path of seeing — a question of how moments are counted within one path; neither school states this reconciliation.
notes: The Tibetan and Dunhuang accounts of Samye differ and are both recorded; neither is adopted.

question: Is the ultimate empty of its own nature like all phenomena (rang stong, self-emptiness), or empty only of what is other than it — the adventitious stains — while not empty of its own nature and qualities (gzhan stong, other-emptiness)?

sides.position: Dolpopa: buddha-nature — the dharmakāya, the dharmadhātu — is the ultimate truth; it is empty of all conventional phenomena, which are adventitious and other than it, but not empty of its own nature (other-emptiness). Conventional phenomena are empty of their own nature, like a rabbit's horns. An emptiness that is nothing whatsoever is annihilatory emptiness and not the ultimate. The final-wheel sūtras, the Maitreya treatises and the Kālacakra teach the definitive meaning; the dharmakāya is the supreme self.

Tāranātha: the thoroughly established nature is self-aware, self-illuminating primordial wisdom free of subject and object, unchanging, realized in meditative equipoise and not empty of itself; self- and other-emptiness agree that all conventional phenomena are empty of own-nature and differ over the ultimate — with twenty-one further differences following.

Tsongkhapa and Khedrup Je: nothing whatsoever, the ultimate included, is established by its own nature; the ultimate truth is the mere absence of inherent existence, a non-affirming negation, and emptiness itself is empty. An ultimate that is truly established, permanent and empty only of other would be an object of grasping at true existence — the extreme of permanence, like the self of the non-Buddhists; the Saṃdhinirmocana's three natures do not teach such an ultimate.

Gorampa: three views are held in Tibet to be Madhyamaka — the eternalist extreme (Dolpopa: the ultimate empty of other but not of itself), the nihilist extreme (Tsongkhapa: the ultimate as mere negation of true existence) — and the Madhyamaka free from all extremes, which is Nāgārjuna's; clinging to emptiness as mere negation is itself an extreme.
Rangjung Dorje: the beginningless element, basis of all phenomena and of nirvāṇa, is mind's nature, luminous and empty, obscured by adventitious stains.

Mipham: buddha-nature is the union of luminosity and emptiness — its emptiness keeps it from being an existent self, its luminosity means the qualities are primordially present; 'other-emptiness' as the Nyingma accept it — the ultimate wisdom empty of adventitious conditioned phenomena — does not conflict with self-emptiness, since that ultimate too is not established by its own nature.

Jamgön Kongtrul: the self-emptiness Madhyamaka of Nāgārjuna's reasonings and the other-emptiness Great Madhyamaka of the Maitreya treatises are each valid in their own sphere — the self-empty approach cuts through elaboration in study and reflection, the other-empty view suits meditative experience; the element is empty of separable stains and not empty of inseparable qualities.

The Indian scriptural ground cited by both sides: the tathāgatagarbha is empty of the separable defilements and not empty of the inseparable buddha-qualities (Śrīmālādevī); nothing is to be removed from it and nothing added (Ratnagotravibhāga 1.154-155); yet the Laṅkāvatāra says the tathāgatagarbha is taught meaning emptiness, not the tīrthika self.

historical_debates.name: Dolpopa's other-emptiness and its Tibetan reception
historical_debates.accounts: Mountain Doctrine and Fourth Council (Dolpopa); Legs bshad snying po and the Tong thun chen mo (Gelug critiques); lta ba'i shan 'byed (Gorampa); Tāranātha's twenty-one differences. In the 17th century Jonang monasteries in central Tibet were converted to the Gelug under the Ganden Phodrang government and Jonang works restricted (historical and tradition accounts; details moderate confidence); other-emptiness was later re-transmitted through the Rimé movement.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jonang: other-emptiness is the definitive Great Madhyamaka; Gelug: other-emptiness is not Madhyamaka; Sakya (Gorampa): both Dolpopa and Tsongkhapa fall to extremes; Rimé: each valid in its sphere.

reconciliation.explanation: Partly reconciled in the Rimé and Nyingma traditions' own terms — self-emptiness for cutting elaboration in study and reflection, other-emptiness for meditative experience (Kongtrul), and other-emptiness understood as not self-established compatible with self-emptiness (Mipham); the Jonang–Gelug disagreement over whether the ultimate is truly established remains not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: P4-stage: Kongtrul assigns the two views to the phases of study/reflection and meditation. P3-path: the analytic temperament and the contemplative (practice-lineage) temperament. Tāranātha himself states the common ground (all conventional phenomena self-empty; elaboration ceases in equipoise) before the differences.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Gelug (Tsongkhapa; Khedrup Je): a truly established ultimate is eternalism like the tīrthika self — no reconciliation. Jonang (Dolpopa): self-emptiness applied to the ultimate is annihilatory emptiness. Sakya (Gorampa): both are extremes. Tāranātha lists twenty-one differences, so the Jonang do not accept that the two views differ only in phase of practice.

candidate_readings: P5-neyartha: which wheel is definitive — the second (emptiness) or the third (buddha-nature) — decides the matter (dsp:which-turning-is-definitive); the parties apply the provisional/definitive distinction in opposite directions.
P1-level (Dolpopa's own assignment): conventional phenomena self-empty, the ultimate other-empty — rejected by Gelug, for whom the ultimate too is empty of own-nature.
P4-stage (Kongtrul): self-emptiness in study, other-emptiness in meditation — accepted in Rimé and much Kagyu and Nyingma teaching, rejected by Gelug and by strict Jonang.

question: Should a Mādhyamika establish emptiness by autonomous inferences (svatantra-anumāna) or only by consequences (prasaṅga) that expose the opponent's own contradictions — and does this difference of method reflect a difference of view?

sides.position: Buddhapālita: things do not arise from themselves, because their arising would be pointless (what already exists need not arise again) and would never end — the argument proceeds by drawing out consequences (prasaṅga) of the opponent's thesis.
sides.tibetan_classification: Prāsaṅgika (thal 'gyur ba) — a later Tibetan doxographic label

sides.position: Bhāviveka: Buddhapālita's argument is inadequate — it states no reason and example, does not answer the faults the opponent would raise, and being a consequence it implies by reversal that things arise from another, against the Mādhyamika's own tenet. The Mādhyamika should state an independent inference: 'ultimately the inner sense-bases do not arise from themselves, because they exist, like consciousness'.
sides.tibetan_classification: Svātantrika (rang rgyud pa) — a later Tibetan doxographic label

sides.position: Candrakīrti: for one who is a Mādhyamika it is not right to state an autonomous inference, since he accepts no other position; as Āryadeva said, one who has no position — existent, non-existent or both — cannot be refuted; Nāgārjuna: 'if I had a thesis the fault would be mine; I have none'. Consequences suffice to show the opponent his own contradictions; Buddhapālita was right.
sides.tibetan_classification: Prāsaṅgika — a later Tibetan doxographic label

sides.position: Śāntarakṣita: entities lack own-nature because they are neither one nor many, like a reflection; the conventional is what is agreeable only when unexamined; relying on mind-only one sees there are no external things, relying on the Middle Way that even mind lacks self — riding both vehicles one reaches the Mahāyāna.
sides.tibetan_classification: Yogācāra-Svātantrika — a later Tibetan doxographic label

sides.position: Tsongkhapa: the difference is one of view, not only of method — the Svātantrikas accept that things have their own character conventionally and therefore use inferences whose subject appears alike to both parties; the Prāsaṅgikas accept no inherent nature even conventionally, so no such common subject exists and they lead the opponent by consequences and inferences 'renowned to the other'; Prāsaṅgika is the higher view, and the object of negation must be identified exactly.

Gorampa: Tsongkhapa's adding of the qualifier 'inherently/truly' to what is negated is not in Nāgārjuna and Candrakīrti, who negate arising and existence without qualification; the Madhyamaka ultimate is freedom from all four extremes, and the negation of true existence alone is only a step.

Mipham: for the provisional, enumerated ultimate, emptiness as the negation of true existence is taught (the Svātantrika emphasis); the actual, non-enumerated ultimate is freedom from all elaboration (the Prāsaṅgika emphasis); from the standpoint of that ultimate there is no thesis to hold, while conventionally the Mādhyamika asserts; the two are to be approached in sequence.

historical_debates.name: The Buddhapālita–Bhāviveka–Candrakīrti exchange on MMK 1.1
historical_debates.accounts: Buddhapālita-vṛtti 1.1; Bhāviveka's Prajñāpradīpa 1.1 criticises it; Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā 1.1 defends Buddhapālita and criticises Bhāviveka's use of autonomous inference.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Indian: Candrakīrti had few Indian followers until Jayānanda and others (scholarly account, labelled); in Tibet his defence became the defining text of Prāsaṅgika.

historical_debates.name: The Tibetan construction of the categories Prāsaṅgika and Svātantrika (metadata)
historical_debates.accounts: The labels thal 'gyur ba (Prāsaṅgika) and rang rgyud pa (Svātantrika) are Tibetan doxographic categories, commonly associated with the translation of Candrakīrti's works in the 11th–12th c. (Pa tshab Nyi ma grags); the Indian authors did not use them as names of schools. Recorded here as metadata only: this entry does not treat the categories as Indian self-designations.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Gelug: Prāsaṅgika the highest view and different in view; Sakya (Gorampa) and Nyingma (Mipham): the difference concerns method and the approach to the ultimate, stated in varying ways.

historical_debates.name: Gelug monastic debate on the Madhyamaka (tradition's account)
historical_debates.accounts: In the Gelug monastic colleges the Madhyamaka is studied through Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra with Tsongkhapa's commentaries and the colleges' own textbooks, and the Prāsaṅgika–Svātantrika distinction is argued in formal courtyard debate (tradition's account; details moderate confidence).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Gelug: the curriculum upholds Tsongkhapa's account.

historical_debates.name: Mipham's exchanges with Gelug scholars
historical_debates.accounts: Replies and counter-replies over Mipham's commentary on Bodhicaryāvatāra ch. 9 (Norbu Ketaka) and the Beacon of Certainty (see dsp:mipham-gelug-madhyamaka, U45).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Nyingma: Mipham's reading stands; Gelug respondents defended Tsongkhapa.

reconciliation.explanation: Partly reconciled in the Nyingma and Sakya traditions' own terms: the Svātantrika approach addresses the enumerated ultimate as a step and the Prāsaṅgika the non-enumerated freedom from extremes (P4-stage), and whether one argues by autonomous inference or by consequence is a matter of how the opponent is led (P6-upaya); the Gelug position that the two differ in view — acceptance of own-character conventionally — is not reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: All the Indian parties agree that nothing arises from self, other, both or neither (MMK 1.1); the Indian exchange concerns method. The Tibetan schools disagree whether the method difference entails a difference in view. The categories themselves are Tibetan (recorded as metadata above).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Candrakīrti: a Mādhyamika should not use autonomous inference at all (Prasannapadā 1.1); Bhāviveka: consequences alone are faulty (Prajñāpradīpa 1.1); Tsongkhapa: Svātantrikas leave a subtle object of negation unrefuted — a difference of view that a stage or skilful-means reading erases; Gorampa rejects Tsongkhapa's qualifier.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: Svātantrika speaks from the standpoint of conventional valid cognition shared with the opponent, Prāsaṅgika from the standpoint of the ultimate with no thesis — rejected by Tsongkhapa as blurring a real difference of view.
P5-neyartha: the Svātantrika presentation as provisional, the Prāsaṅgika as definitive — the Gelug ranking, which Svātantrika authors themselves would not accept.
notes: Per the brief, the Tibetan construction of the categories Prāsaṅgika/Svātantrika is recorded as metadata (see the historical_debates entry marked metadata and each side's 'tibetan_classification'); Indian authors are placed under lin:madhyamaka / lin:yogacara-madhyamaka rather than under the Tibetan category lineages.

question: Is liberation won by ritual works, by knowledge alone, by knowledge combined with works, by devotion, or by the Lord's grace — and does grace wait on the soul's surrender (the 'monkey') or carry it without cause (the 'cat')?

sides.position: Dharma, known only from the Veda, yields its fruit; liberation is not enjoined as a fruit of ritual knowledge. For one who knows the self, when earlier actions are exhausted by experience and no new ones arise — by avoiding desire-prompted and forbidden acts and performing the obligatory ones — there is no further embodiment (Kumārila). The self is subsidiary to the rite as its agent (the prior view in BS 3.4.2).

One troubled by the sorrows of transmigration, not longing even for its pleasures, who gives up enjoined and forbidden acts and exhausts past merit and demerit, attains the self's abiding free of the qualities — liberation.

Knowledge alone liberates: liberation is not something produced, reached, modified or purified by action but the eternal nature of the self; knowledge of an existing thing depends on the thing, not on the person's will; action is not opposed to ignorance and cannot remove it. Works done without desire purify the mind and produce the desire to know (sacrifice, gifts and austerity, BĀU 4.4.22) and are then renounced; knowledge cannot be combined with works, since works require the notions of agent, act and fruit that knowledge removes.

Bhāskara (and before him Bhartṛprapañca): knowledge must be combined with the lifelong performance of prescribed works (jñāna-karma-samuccaya); 'then' in 'then the inquiry into Brahman' means after the inquiry into ritual; release does not come while the body lasts.

Liberating knowledge is not the understanding of a sentence but meditation — continuous, loving remembrance (bhakti) — to which works and knowledge are ancillary; the inquiry into Brahman follows the inquiry into ritual. Or, for those unable, the Lord's own words 'abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone' teach surrender (prapatti).

Vedānta Deśika: surrender (prapatti) is an independent means the soul performs once, with its limbs, and is the occasion of the Lord's grace — as the young monkey clings to its mother (the 'monkey' analogy, markaṭa-nyāya).

Piḷḷai Lokācārya: the Lord alone is the means; surrender is not a means but the acceptance befitting the soul's dependence; his grace is without cause — as the mother cat carries the kitten (the 'cat' analogy, mārjāra-nyāya).
sides.notes: The cat/monkey labels are the traditions' own mnemonic summaries of the difference; the texts argue it in terms of upāya.

sides.position: Without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation, and without knowledge no abundant grace: grace won by ritual action is the lowest, by hearing and reflection middling, by direct vision the highest; liberation is won by his pleasure alone, with love preceded by knowledge of his greatness.

Devotion is greater than action, knowledge and yoga, being of the nature of the fruit; neither yoga, Sāṃkhya, dharma, study, austerity nor renunciation wins the Lord as strong devotion does; devotion is not an act, since like knowledge it does not depend on effort.

The Gītā: a twofold commitment was declared of old — the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, the yoga of action for the yogins; renunciation and the yoga of action both bring the highest good; Janaka reached perfection by action; the sacrifice of knowledge is better than material sacrifice; not by the Vedas, austerity, gifts or sacrifice but by exclusive devotion can the Lord be seen; performing all actions, taking refuge in him, one attains by his grace; 'abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone'.

The Upaniṣads cited by every side: the self is not attained by instruction, intellect or much learning but by the one whom it chooses; sacrifices are unsafe boats; those who worship ignorance (ritual) enter darkness, and greater darkness those delighting in knowledge alone — by both one crosses death; brāhmaṇas seek to know the self by Veda-study, sacrifice, gifts and austerity.

Ignorance — not mere absence of knowledge but incomplete manifestation — is the cause of transmigration and knowledge the sole cause of liberation; the descent of power (śaktipāta) depends on the Lord's freedom alone, not on a balance of karma, and is intense, middling or mild; initiation leading to nirvāṇa happens for the one who knows this, without oblation.

Bondage by āṇava-mala is a real substance that knowledge alone cannot remove; when the two deeds are balanced and mala has ripened, grace descends and the guru, as Śiva, removes the bonds in initiation — the rite liberates by Śiva's power.

Right view, right knowledge and right conduct together are the path to liberation; knowledge without action is lost and the action of the ignorant is lost. No creator's grace is admitted: the soul frees itself.

In an age without a buddha one cannot reach non-retrogression by self-power; birth in the Pure Land is by the power of Amitābha's vow (other-power); Shinran: even the good are born there, how much more the evil — shinjin and the nembutsu are themselves given.

historical_debates.name: Śaṅkara and Maṇḍana Miśra at Māhiṣmatī
historical_debates.accounts: Śaṅkaradigvijaya 8–10 (the tradition's account): the debate on knowledge versus Vedic ritual, judged by Maṇḍana's wife Ubhaya Bhāratī, who placed a garland on each; Maṇḍana's garland withered first.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita tradition: Maṇḍana accepted that knowledge alone liberates, took renunciation, and became Sureśvara.
historical_debates.scholarly: The identity of Maṇḍana Miśra with Sureśvara is disputed (scholarly account, labelled); Maṇḍana's own Brahmasiddhi holds works helpful to knowledge (see dsp:jnana-karma-samuccaya).

historical_debates.name: The division of the Vaṭakalai and Teṅkalai
historical_debates.accounts: Vedānta Deśika's Rahasyatrayasāra; Piḷḷai Lokācārya's Śrīvacana Bhūṣaṇam and Mumukṣuppaḍi with Maṇavāḷa Māmuni's commentaries; the traditions list eighteen differences (see dsp:vadakalai-tenkalai).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Both traditions continue; each holds its account of prapatti and grace to be Rāmānuja's.

historical_debates.name: Hōnen at Ōhara
historical_debates.accounts: Hōnen Shōnin Gyōjō Ezu: before Tendai and Nara scholars Hōnen explained birth by the nembutsu of the vow for ordinary beings of this age.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Jōdo tradition: the scholars were persuaded.

reconciliation.explanation: Reconciled in part by the texts' own ordering: works purify the mind and produce the desire to know (P4-stage — Advaita, Bhāmatī), the Gītā's two commitments for two kinds of people and the Uddhava Gītā's three yogas for different temperaments (P3-path); whether knowledge alone or knowledge with works finally liberates, whether devotion is a means or the goal beyond liberation, and whether grace takes the soul's surrender as its condition remain not yet reconciled.
reconciliation.detail: P4: BSBh 3.4.26 and the Bhāmatī make works a preliminary to knowledge; Rāmānuja makes karma- and jñāna-yoga ancillary to bhakti; Madhva grades grace by the means that wins it. P3: BhG 3.3 ('a twofold commitment'), Uddhava Gītā 11.20.6-8 ('knowledge, action and devotion — there is no other'). What is not reconciled: samuccaya (Bhāskara) vs knowledge alone (Śaṅkara); Mīmāṃsā's liberation by exhausting karma vs Vedānta's knowledge; prapatti as a means (Vaṭakalai) vs no means (Teṅkalai); self-power vs other-power; grace by the Lord's freedom (Trika) vs grace occasioned by ripened mala (Siddhānta).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Śaṅkara rejects samuccaya (Gītā-bhāṣya intro to 2.11; BĀU-bhāṣya 5.1.1); Bhāskara rejects knowledge alone; the bhakti schools deny that devotion is merely preparatory (NBS 25-26); the Teṅkalai deny that surrender is a means, the Vaṭakalai affirm it; Jōdo Shinshū denies any self-power; the Jains admit no grace.

candidate_readings: P8-six-marks: the Gītā's purport by opening and close — knowledge (Śaṅkara, from 2.11 and 18.66 as renunciation), devotion (Rāmānuja, Madhusūdana's closing verse), action (recent readings) — see dsp:gita-primary-teaching.

P7-arthavada: praise of works, of knowledge or of devotion as 'greater than all others' read as praise rather than exclusive doctrine — each school reads the others' texts so and rejects that reading of its own.
P1-level: works valid at the empirical level, knowledge alone at the ultimate — Advaita's own form, rejected by Bhāskara and by the bhakti schools.

cat and monkey (P2-standpoint): from the Lord's side grace is causeless, from the soul's side surrender is its fitting response — offered within Śrīvaiṣṇavism but not accepted as dissolving the eighteen differences.

question: Is there an Īśvara — a Lord who makes the world and dispenses the fruits of action? Is he proved by reason, known only from scripture, a special puruṣa for meditation, or not to be accepted at all?

sides.position: There is an all-knowing, imperishable maker (Īśvara): the world is an effect, like a pot, so it has an intelligent maker; the combination of atoms, the support of the world, the arts and the Veda's authority require him; he brings about the fruit of human effort according to karma (Udayana answers five objections in five clusters).

At the end of Brahmā's life Maheśvara, wishing to give rest to beings wearied by transmigration, dissolves the world, and at his will creation begins again from the atoms according to the unseen merit of souls.

Īśvara is a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruition and residues, in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed; devotion to him (praṇidhāna) brings samādhi near, since won over by it he favours the yogin — a model and a support, not the world's maker.

Īśvara is not established: whether free or bound he could not create; unconscious prakṛti acts for puruṣa's release as unconscious milk flows for the calf; the fruit of action comes from karma without a governor.

There is no creator: no time without action is known; with no beings yet there would be none to pity, and a compassionate creator would make only happy beings; the Veda needs no author; in the rite the sacrifice, not the deity, is principal, and dharma itself yields the fruit.

Brahman as Lord is the cause of the world's origin, maintenance and dissolution, known from scripture alone — the Veda is breathed out by him; he is not partial or cruel, since like rain he gives according to the seeds of beings' karma; the fruit of works comes from him. (Īśvara belongs to Brahman as related to adjuncts.)
Inference cannot prove a single omniscient maker of the world; Brahman, the Lord with infinite auspicious qualities, qualified by souls and matter, is known only from scripture (śāstrayonitvāt).
Viṣṇu alone is the independent reality from whom come creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release.
The world undergoes origination, maintenance and dissolution and so has an agent; unconscious māyā and karma cannot organize themselves to give each soul its due, so an omniscient Lord is required.

There is no permanent means of knowledge or permanent cause: what is permanent cannot produce effects successively; 'being an effect' does not prove a single intelligent maker of mountains and sprouts; the Blessed One is a means of knowledge by having become so, not as an eternal lord (Dharmakīrti, Śāntarakṣita, Ratnakīrti). Belief in Īśvara as cause arises from the error of a permanent self (Vasubandhu).
There is no god, no Brahmā, who makes this round of rebirths; only bare dhammas occur through the conjunction of conditions; the wheel of becoming is without a maker.

The maker-god of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika cannot be: an unembodied maker cannot act, an embodied one would be limited; if he made the world, where was he before and what was his material? — obstinate fancies. Haribhadra: the doctrine that Īśvara is the maker can be accepted in a true sense — the soul that reaches the highest state, whose teaching leads beings, is Īśvara.
Some sages say inherent nature is the cause, others time — they are deluded; it is the greatness of God in the world; 'we have found him, the supreme great Lord of lords'.
(As reported) The only lord is the king known to the world; variety comes from own-nature.
Those who say the world was made by gods, Brahmā, Īśvara, pradhāna or the self-born do not know the truth; the world never perishes.
If Brahmā were lord of the world, why did he make it unhappy and unjust? Creation by God is a tenet that ends in inaction.

historical_debates.name: The Nyāya–Buddhist exchange on proofs of the Lord (textual)
historical_debates.accounts: Nyāyavārttika on NS 4.1.19-21; Pramāṇavārttika (Pramāṇasiddhi); Tattvasaṅgraha (Īśvaraparīkṣā); Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali; Ratnakīrti's Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each tradition holds its own arguments stand.
historical_debates.notes: Written replies across generations; direct reply between particular works is not asserted.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Śaiva Siddhānta affirm a Lord (by inference or by scripture), Yoga admits a special puruṣa for devotion but not as maker, and Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā, the Buddhists and the Jains reject a creator.
reconciliation.detail: A partial agreement cutting across the sides: Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta (BS 1.1.3; Śrībhāṣya 1.1.3) and the Buddhists concur that inference cannot establish a world-maker — for opposite ends. Haribhadra offers a Jain reinterpretation (the perfected soul as 'Īśvara').
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Nyāya holds the inference sound (Kusumāñjali 5.1); the Buddhists, Jains, Mīmāṃsakas and Sāṃkhyas each give explicit refutations; Yoga's Īśvara is rejected by the non-theistic Sāṃkhya (see dsp:yoga-samkhya-isvara); Advaita places the Lord at the level of Brahman with adjuncts, which the theistic schools reject.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint (Haribhadra's own): 'Īśvara is the maker' true in the sense that the soul reaching the highest state is Īśvara and its teaching shapes beings — rejected by Nyāya, whose Lord is eternally free, and not a creator in the Jain sense.

P3-path (Yoga): devotion to Īśvara as one of the means ('or', YS 1.23) for those of devotional temperament, without deciding creation — the non-theistic Sāṃkhya and the Buddhists do not accept an Īśvara even as an object of devotion.

P1-level (Advaita): the Lord is real at the empirical level (Brahman with adjuncts), transcended in the ultimate — rejected by the theistic Vedāntas and the Śaivas, for whom the Lord is ultimately real.
notes: Cārvāka, Jain (Sūtrakṛtāṅga) and early Buddhist (Bhūridatta Jātaka) sides contributed by U33 are included verbatim.
